messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Park Ranger
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 41

# Case Vignette: Daniel

Daniel is a 32-year-old park ranger who works in a remote wilderness preserve in the Pacific Northwest. He is quiet and deliberate in the way he speaks, choosing his words carefully, pausing often — a habit that feels less like thoughtfulness and more like he is listening for something just beyond the room. He has been single for the past two years, and when asked about this, he shrugs and says only that it is easier that way.

Three years ago, Daniel was taken captive during a solo backcountry trip that crossed into a remote stretch of land near the Canadian border. He had stumbled upon what he later understood to be an illegal grow operation. The men who found him held him for four days in a outbuilding on the property. During that time, he was bound, beaten repeatedly, deprived of sleep, and subjected to prolonged periods of what he can only describe as "things I won't talk about in detail" — episodes of deliberate, methodical pain inflicted to keep him compliant and terrified. He survived because a search party, alerted by a missed check-in, eventually located the property. He was airlifted out with two broken ribs, lacerations, and a dislocated shoulder. The men were arrested. There was a trial. Daniel testified and then tried, as he puts it, "to move on."

Moving on has not gone the way he expected. In the months after his release, he returned to work as quickly as he could, believing the familiar rhythms of the forest — the trail assessments, the wildlife monitoring, the long solitary days — would restore him. For stretches of time, they almost do. But the wilderness that once felt like home now carries an undercurrent of threat he cannot fully silence. When he is deep in the backcountry, far from radio contact, his body goes on alert in a way that has nothing to do with professional caution. His chest tightens. He scans tree lines not for wildlife but for movement that shouldn't be there. Twice in the past year he has had to sit down on a trail and press his back against a tree trunk, breathing deliberately, waiting for his heart rate to drop.

At night, sleep is unreliable. He wakes in the early hours with his hands clenched and a specific, physical memory of being restrained — not a dream exactly, more like a sensation that has bypassed his mind and landed directly in his body. He lies still until it passes, which sometimes takes an hour. He has stopped mentioning this to anyone because the one time he did, a coworker told him he was lucky to be alive, and Daniel found he had nothing to say in response to that.

He is irritable in ways that embarrass him. Small frustrations — a piece of equipment that won't cooperate, a hiker who ignores trail rules — can produce a flash of anger that feels disproportionate and foreign, like it belongs to someone else. He has become more isolated, declining the informal gatherings his ranger station organizes, finding excuses not to visit his family in Oregon. His younger sister has noticed and calls more often than she used to. He answers when he can manage it.

What Daniel finds most difficult to articulate is not the fear or the sleeplessness but a subtler loss — the sense that the person who walked into that backcountry three years ago and the person who walked out are not quite the same man. He still loves his work. He still believes in it. But there are moments, standing alone in a clearing with the light coming through the canopy, when he feels a distance between himself and the world around him that he cannot close, no matter how long he stands there.
